6-18.title: Don’t rely on generic health check packages to prevent disease; get the age- and sex-appropriate screening instead
6-18.cost: There is no cost at all, and you save the price of a package each year. The trade-off is remembering which tests you actually need and how often to have them.
6-18.inPlainWords: People who go through general health checks die at the same rate as people who do not, including from heart disease and cancer. What pays is the screening that matches your age and sex. In India the free public route is the Ayushman Arogya Mandir, the health and wellness centre, which screens adults from age 30 for high blood pressure, diabetes and the three common cancers, and takes a blood pressure reading at the visit. What India does not have is a nationwide free annual full-body check with an abdominal ultrasound for everyone over 65; where a hospital or a state scheme offers one, it is local, not a national entitlement.
6-18.benefit: The 2019 update of a Cochrane systematic review pooled 17 randomised controlled trials. For overall mortality, 11 trials with 233,298 participants and 21,535 deaths found no difference: RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.97-1.03). For cardiovascular deaths, nine trials with 170,227 participants and 6,237 deaths gave RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94-1.16); for cancer deaths, eight trials with 139,290 participants and 3,663 deaths gave RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.92-1.12). None of these differences was meaningful, and the authors concluded that general health checks are unlikely to deliver real benefit. The Indian public route to screening is different in design: the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke, delivered through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, offers a risk-factor questionnaire, blood pressure, blood sugar and screening for oral, breast and cervical cancer from age 30, with referral upward for anyone who screens positive. That is a targeted programme, not an annual package, and it does not include an abdominal ultrasound for the over-65s.
6-18.caveats: What this discourages is buying annual check-up packages as prevention; it does not mean skipping tests. The NCD screening at a government health and wellness centre is free and worth using, but it is a different thing from a paid package and it does not include an ultrasound. Get tested for anything you have a reason to screen for. Blood pressure, blood sugar and hepatitis B are in Chapter 1, Rules 7, 8 and 14; breast, cervical and colorectal cancer screening in Rules 17, 18 and 19; Helicobacter pylori testing and low-dose CT in Rules 23 and 24; bone density for women over 65 in Rule 39; and high-risk exposure in Rule 31, where the recommended ages and intervals are listed. Attend any employer or insurer screening you are offered; the warning is about buying full packages or adding tests at your own expense. People with a chronic disease, symptoms, or a test ordered by a doctor are outside this advice - that is treatment, not screening. The tests most often sold with little or no evidence behind them are tumour markers and whole-body imaging; see Rule 7 for PET-CT and marker panels. For high uric acid or silent gallstones see Rules 19 and 20. Most of the Cochrane trials ran in high-income countries where care is easy to reach, so the conclusion may not transfer cleanly to a district with one CT scanner.

caveats: Legally, involuntary hospitalization is permitted only

Legally, the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 sets the only route for admitting an adult to a psychiatric facility against their wishes, and it is narrower than “seems to be a risk”. Admission as a supported patient under section 89, for up to thirty days, requires two independent examinations — one by a psychiatrist, the other by a psychiatrist, a mental health professional or a medical practitioner — each concluding that the person has a mental illness of such severity that they have recently threatened, attempted or are threatening to cause bodily harm to themselves, or have recently behaved violently towards another person or caused another person to fear bodily harm, or are unable to care for themselves to a degree that places them at risk of harm. It also requires that admission is the least restrictive option available, that the person is unable to make mental healthcare decisions independently and needs very high support, and that a nominated representative is appointed. Anyone admitted without that paperwork can challenge the admission before the Mental Health Review Board. No Indian statute bans conversion therapy outright; the Indian Psychiatric Society's position and the National Medical Commission's professional-conduct regulations treat it as improper practice rather than a criminal offence, so the protection here is professional discipline and civil liability, not prosecution.

6-35.inPlainWords: A drip is a medical procedure with real risks, not a tonic. No infusion of saline, vitamins or “antioxidants” flushes away or dissolves the plaques in your arteries; the artery wall is protected over years by blood pressure and lipid control. Extra intravenous fluid strains the heart and kidneys, and can precipitate heart failure in someone with heart disease. Indian guidance on rational use of medicines and antibiotic stewardship points the same way - a common cold or an uncomplicated viral throat infection does not need an outpatient infusion - but clinics and “wellness” centres sell them anyway, which is why you have to ask what the drip is for.
6-35.benefit: The principle is simple and the World Health Organization states it plainly: never inject when oral medication is possible; never infuse intravenously when intramuscular injection is possible. An intravenous infusion is clinically justified in three situations: an inability to swallow; severe gastrointestinal malabsorption, with persistent vomiting or severe diarrhoea; or a critical, rapidly progressing illness that needs a high drug concentration in the blood at once. A common cold, an uncomplicated sore throat or a seasonal “flush” is none of those. Infusions cannot dislodge or clear atherosclerotic plaques; unindicated fluid loading risks circulatory volume overload, cardiac strain and acute heart failure. India has no nationwide directive that designates outpatient drip clinics off limits. The standard comes instead from professional regulation: the National Medical Commission's professional-conduct regulations require the rational use of medicines, hospital antimicrobial-stewardship committees review what is prescribed, and the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India collects reports of adverse drug reactions — in which injections feature far more heavily than oral medicines.

6-20.caveats: This topic is still debated. The exact criteria for those exceptions haven’t been verified yet. Another counterpoint concerns small stones: those under 5 mm are more closely linked to pancreatitis, and Dutch research suggests prophylactic removal might either extend or shorten life depending on how common and severe pancreatitis is in a given population. European guidelines do list two exceptions: porcelain gallbladder and gallstones over 1 cm alongside large polyps — both warrant removal. Removal may also be considered during other major abdominal surgeries. Crucially, this advice applies only to stones inside the gallbladder with no prior symptoms; stones in the common bile duct are a completely different matter. UK and European guidelines both stress that stones in the bile duct must be removed along with the gallbladder, regardless of symptoms. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience persistent upper abdominal pain, fever, chills, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or dark urine. When a doctor recommends surgery after reviewing imaging, ask which specific criteria prompted that decision — whether it’s bile duct involvement, polyps, or abnormal gallbladder walls — so you can weigh those factors against this general guideline, which is meant to discourage surgery without any valid medical reason. Both cited studies tracked patients over 4 to 9 years, focusing on what happens when no intervention is taken; they don’t compare treatment effectiveness. Longer follow-ups would likely show a higher rate of symptom development.

6-22.caveats: This entry serves one main purpose: to emphasize that there is no scientific basis for any claimed benefits, nor any measurable predictive power. It does not pass judgment on personal beliefs or cultural traditions, nor does it discourage buying such items as gifts, mementos, or family heirlooms. Two points must be clearly distinguished: legally enforceable claims about product performance can be reported to authorities, while vague notions like “good luck” lack any research support and cannot be proven false; thus, personal budget control is the only practical safeguard. Before purchasing, treat the item strictly as a decorative piece and ask yourself: “If it offered no magical benefits at all, would I still pay this price?” For guidance on verifying materials and certifications, or why treating them as investments is unwise, refer to Sections 5.33 and 5.34. Information on spending money on fortune-tellers is provided in Section 5.15.
6-22.title: Don’t buy crystals, bracelets or “lucky” figurines for good luck, wealth or health benefits
6-22.inPlainWords: There is no verifiable evidence that wearing such an item changes your fate, attracts wealth or improves health. The claims work the way fortune-telling does: they are vague enough that anyone can read themselves into them. Where a seller states outright that a stone cures a disease or guarantees money, that is a misleading advertisement under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and can be complained about to the Central Consumer Protection Authority or a district consumer commission; vague talk of “good luck” is not something any authority can prove false. Buying such an item as decoration is fine; paying extra for the luck is what this entry is about.

6-17.caveats: This entry does not oppose blood donation itself, but the notion that it is a personal health practice. The blood goes to other people, and under this book’s classification of beneficiaries that is category 4, strangers. India has no national scheme that waives your own future hospital fees or gives you free transport in return for donating; some states and blood banks operate a replacement arrangement, and hospitals may waive processing charges for a donor, but none of that is a right you can rely on. Eligibility is decided by the blood centre, not by you: Indian blood-bank rules set a minimum weight, a minimum haemoglobin level and a minimum gap between whole-blood donations, and the centre is required to check them. Do not shorten the interval to meet an honour target or a camp’s collection goal. Women, people with low body weight and women with heavy periods start with smaller iron reserves; a regular donor may want a ferritin test. If persistent fatigue, cold intolerance or restless legs appear after donation, that is likely iron deficiency rather than “loss of vitality” - get a blood count and a ferritin level, take iron if advised, and lengthen the interval. The cold-intolerance evidence comes from a single study of 2,024 participants and is quoted to show the phenomenon exists, not to say how common it is.

6-3.cost: Roughly ₹3 to ₹7 per day, or ₹1,400 to ₹2,800 per year. That's not much money, but the real cost is the false sense of security it gives — the belief that you've already taken preventive steps.

6-4.cost: Roughly ₹7 to ₹28 per day. For smokers, the real cost is a higher risk of lung cancer.

6-6.cost: Each effervescent tablet costs roughly ₹14–₹28; annual expense ranges from ₹4,300 to ₹9,900.

6-7.cost: A whole-body PET-CT costs roughly ₹15,000–₹35,000 per scan at a private centre, and exposes you to ionizing radiation. Tumour marker panels cost a few thousand rupees. The real cost comes later: when an “abnormality” is found — usually a false positive — follow-up tests, biopsies, and surgeries add up both financially and physically.

6-8.cost: Devices cost between ₹2,800 and ₹28,400. Plus, you have to constantly pay attention to the data they display every day.

inPlainWords: The price isn’t just a few dollars
The price isn’t measured in rupees alone: a free reading ends with a demand for “offering fees” or “donation packages”, and the sums climb.
benefit: Official records show a similar pattern

The commercial version follows the same script: a free reading, then “offering fees” and “donation packages” once the customer is drawn in. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a seller who states outright that such a service will cure an illness or guarantee money is making a misleading claim, which can be complained about to the Central Consumer Protection Authority or to a district consumer commission.
